messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan never spoke about what happened the night of the charity gala. He was sixty-three then, working as a fundraiser for a small non-profit that supported refugee resettlement. He had stayed late to help clean up, and a colleague he had trusted for years offered him a ride home. Instead, the man drove him to a deserted warehouse district, where he raped him in the back seat of the car. Rajan did not report it. He told himself it was a misunderstanding, that he had misread the situation, that real men would have fought back. He had come to believe that his reaction since then—the freezing, the silence, the inability to say no—proved he was a lousy coper, someone who had failed the most basic test of manhood. That belief, that he was permanently broken, became the soil in which everything else grew.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night became a living thing. It had no words—Rajan would sit in his small apartment, knowing what had happened, but unable to form a sentence about it. Instead, the memory came as sound: the click of the car door locking, the zip of his own trousers, the wet breathing of the man above him. It came as pain: a sharp, cramping ache in his lower back and thighs, exactly where he had been pressed into the seat, even when he was lying in bed. These intrusions convinced him he would never feel normal again, that his body and mind had been permanently colonized by that night. The more the memories came, the more he felt like an outsider—someone who no longer belonged in the ordinary world of meetings and grocery stores and polite conversation.

To manage the threat he now sensed everywhere, Rajan developed a set of habits that felt less like choices than survival reflexes. He could not bear to be alone in a room, so he kept his apartment door unlocked and the television on at all hours, even when he was trying to sleep. When he did sit down, he always positioned himself with his back against the wall, scanning the door and windows. He also began to hurt himself physically—digging his fingernails into his forearms until they bled, or pressing a lit cigarette against his thigh—because the sharp, controllable pain released the overwhelming pressure that built inside him when a memory hit. These strategies, he believed, were further proof of his inadequacy. A strong person would not need to cut himself to get through the day.

The threat monitoring consumed him. He reacted with alarm whenever someone touched him unexpectedly—a hand on his shoulder at work sent him flinching into a filing cabinet. He listened obsessively for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home: the creak of the hallway floorboards, the jiggle of the front door handle. Unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring, a dropped tray in the office kitchen—sent his heart racing and his palms slick with sweat. Each startle reinforced his belief that he was a bad coper, that normal people did not live like this, and that he would never recover. The threat also drove more avoidance: he stopped attending evening events, stopped accepting rides from anyone, and began leaving work early to walk home in full daylight, always checking over his shoulder.

The avoidance, in turn, fed the memory. Every time he sat with his back to the wall, every time he flinched at a touch, every time he cut himself to release the pressure, he was reminding himself that something terrible had happened and that he was still in danger. The strategies kept the memory alive, vivid, and intrusive. They also deepened his shame, creating a loop that tightened over the years. By the time he turned sixty-eight, he had been divorced for a decade, his ex-wife having grown exhausted by his hypervigilance and emotional distance. He had lost touch with most of his friends. At work, he was competent but distant, never staying for casual conversation, never accepting the kind gesture of a colleague offering to walk him to his car.

What finally brought Rajan to a clinic was not the memories themselves, nor the cutting, nor the constant scanning of rooms. It was the realization that he could no longer remember what it felt like to be at ease. He had not sat in a chair without checking the exits in five years. He had not let anyone touch him in seven. He had come to believe that the man who raped him had not only taken that night—he had taken every night since. Rajan was afraid that therapy would only confirm what he already suspected: that he was too old, too set in his ways, too broken to change. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life sitting with his back against the wall.
